seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
title: DSA: linked lists, trees and heaps
description: Linked-list pointer surgery (reverse, cycle, nth from end, merge), binary tree traversals, LCA, BST validation, serialization, and heap patterns: top K, merge K lists, running median.
source: LeetCode problem set and discuss; NeetCode roadmap; Cracking the Coding Interview; Oracle Java docs (PriorityQueue, ArrayDeque, Comparator); Python docs (heapq, collections.deque), CPython Counter.most_common source

questions.prompt: Write a Java method ListNode reverse(ListNode head) that reverses a singly linked list iteratively (ListNode has int val and ListNode next) and returns the new head.

checks.label: loops while the current node is not null
saves the next node before rewiring
points the current node back to the previous one
returns the previous pointer as the new head

questions.explanation: Three pointers, O(n) time and O(1) space. A recursive version works too but uses O(n) stack. The classic bug is overwriting cur.next before saving it.

questions.prompt: The list is 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 and node 5 points back to node 3. Slow and fast both start at node 1; each iteration moves slow by 1 and fast by 2. After how many iterations do they first meet?
questions.explanation: Iteration 1: slow 2, fast 3. Iteration 2: slow 3, fast 5. Iteration 3: slow 4, fast moves 5 -> 3 -> 4, meeting at node 4. Floyd: once inside a cycle the gap closes by one each step.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Using a dummy node before the head simplifies "remove the nth node from the end".
questions.reason: Removing the head itself has no predecessor, so without a dummy node it needs a special case.

whys.a: Correct: the dummy gives the head a predecessor, so one code path handles every position.
whys.b: R is the actual reason, so "does not explain" is wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so this is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so this is wrong.

questions.explanation: Two pointers: advance fast n steps from the dummy, then move both until fast.next is null; slow.next is the node to unlink. One pass, O(1) space.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Floyd's tortoise and hare detects a cycle in a linked list with O(1) extra space.
questions.reason: Storing every visited node in a HashSet also detects a cycle, in O(n) time and O(n) space.

whys.a: R describes a different technique and does not explain why Floyd needs only two pointers.
whys.b: Correct: both are true; R is the alternative approach, not the reason Floyd is constant space.
whys.c: A is true, so this is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so this is wrong.

questions.explanation: Mention both: HashSet is easiest to explain, Floyd is the space-optimal follow-up, and phase two (reset one pointer to the head) finds the cycle start.

questions.prompt: A recursive inorder traversal runs on a left-leaning chain of 6 nodes (each node has only a left child). Counting the root call as depth 1 and calls on null children as real calls, what is the greatest number of calls active on the stack at once?
questions.explanation: Six node calls nest to depth 6, and the deepest node calls itself on its null left child, giving 7. With n nodes in a skewed tree the stack grows O(n), which is why Python recursion (default limit 1000) fails on a 100,000-node chain.

questions.prompt: Match each traversal or structure with the job it is best known for.

right.text: Uses a queue and visits nodes depth by depth
Yields the values in sorted order
Visits a node before its children, natural for serializing
Visits children before the node, natural for computing height or size
Uses a min-heap to order the nodes

questions.explanation: DFS orders use recursion or an explicit stack (ArrayDeque); level order uses a queue. Inorder on a BST sorted order is also how you find the kth smallest.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function level_order(root) returning a list of lists of values, one per level, using collections.deque. The node class has val, left and right.
questions.starter:
from collections import deque

def level_order(root):

checks.label: uses a deque as the queue
dequeues from the left in O(1)
processes one level at a time using the queue length
enqueues left and right children when present
returns the result

questions.explanation: Snapshotting len(q) at the start of each level is the trick. A two-list version (current level, next level) also passes. list.pop(0) would be O(n) per pop.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function lca(root, p, q) returning the lowest common ancestor of nodes p and q in a binary tree (both exist; compare nodes with is).

checks.label: returns root on null or when root is p or q
recurses into the left subtree
recurses into the right subtree
returns root when both sides found something

questions.explanation: O(n) time, O(h) stack. For a BST you can instead walk down comparing values with root.val in O(h), which interviewers often ask as the follow-up.

questions.prompt: Which is the standard bug in a validate-BST function that only checks node.left.val < node.val < node.right.val at every node?

options.text: It ignores ancestor bounds, so a deep 4 right of 5 slips by.
options.why: Right: every node must lie in a (low, high) range inherited from all ancestors, so pass bounds down or check inorder is strictly increasing.

options.text: It rejects valid trees that contain duplicate values in a subtree.
options.why: Duplicates are a policy question; the local check does not specifically reject them.

options.text: It runs in O(n^2) because each node re-compares its whole subtree.
options.why: Each node is visited once, so the time is O(n); the problem is correctness.

options.text: It only works when the tree happens to be a complete binary tree.
options.why: Shape is irrelevant; the flaw is local comparison.

questions.explanation: Two correct fixes: recursion with (low, high) bounds, or an inorder walk that remembers the previous value. Use long or None bounds so Integer.MIN_VALUE nodes do not break the check.

questions.prompt: Complete the serialize / deserialize design for a binary tree.
questions.text: Serialize with a {1} traversal and write an explicit {2} marker for each missing child; deserialize by consuming the tokens from a {3} in the same order.
questions.explanation: Preorder plus null markers is unambiguous; preorder alone is not (many trees share one preorder). Level-order with null markers (LeetCode style) also works and uses a queue to rebuild.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Merging K sorted lists with N total nodes using a min-heap of list heads costs O(N log K).
questions.reason: The heap can grow to hold all N nodes at the same time.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, so no both-true option applies.
whys.c: Correct: A is true and the heap holds at most K entries (one head per list), so R is false.
whys.d: A is true, so this is wrong.

questions.explanation: Each of N pops and pushes costs log K. Divide and conquer (merge pairs of lists) reaches the same O(N log K) with O(1) extra space.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function top_k_frequent(nums, k) that returns the k most frequent values using collections.Counter and the heapq module.

checks.label: counts frequencies with Counter
uses heapq (nlargest or a size-k heap with heappush)
orders by the count, e.g. key=count.get or (count, value) tuples
returns the selected values

questions.explanation: O(n log k). Alternatively keep a min-heap of (count, value) of size k and pop when it exceeds k. Bucket sort by frequency is O(n) and a good follow-up.

questions.prompt: A running-median structure keeps the smaller half in a max-heap and the larger half in a min-heap, rebalanced so the max-heap holds equal or one more element. After inserting 1, 2, ..., 9, how many elements are in the max-heap?
questions.explanation: 9 elements split 5 + 4, and the median 5 is the max-heap root. With an even count both heaps have the same size and the median is the average of the two roots. Each insert is O(log n) and the median read is O(1).

questions.prompt: In Java you need a max-heap of int values that may include Integer.MIN_VALUE. Which PriorityQueue construction is safe?

options.why: Right: it compares with compareTo and never overflows.

options.text: new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> b - a) using plain subtraction
options.why: Subtraction can overflow for extreme values, such as MIN_VALUE - 1, and gives the wrong order.

options.text: new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a - b) and read from the tail
options.why: That is also an overflow risk and builds a min-heap anyway.

options.text: new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.max()) with a null comparator
options.why: There is no such constructor; Collections.max returns an element.

questions.explanation: Use Integer.compare(b, a) or Comparator.reverseOrder(). In Python heapq is a min-heap only, so push negated values to simulate a max-heap.

questions.prompt: Building a binary heap from an unsorted array of n elements with heapify (sift-down from the middle) takes O(n), not O(n log n).

options.why: Right: most nodes are near the leaves and sift down only a few levels; the total sums to O(n).
The bound is tighter than n log n; inserting elements one at a time would be n log n.

questions.explanation: This is why PriorityQueue(Collection) and heapq.heapify(list) are preferred over a loop of adds when you already have all the data.

questions.prompt: Iterating over or printing a Java PriorityQueue returns its elements in sorted order.

options.why: Iteration follows the internal array layout, not sorted order, so this is not true.
Right: only poll() is ordered; the internal array is just a heap, e.g. adding 5,1,4,2,3 prints [1, 2, 4, 5, 3].

questions.explanation: Drain with poll() when you need sorted output, which is O(n log n) in total.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function kth_largest(nums, k) returning the k-th largest element (k=1 is the maximum) by keeping a min-heap of size k with heapq.

checks.label: builds a heap
replaces the root when a larger value arrives
reads the heap root as the answer
returns a value

questions.explanation: O(n log k) time and O(k) space; the root of a size-k min-heap is the k-th largest seen so far. Quickselect gives O(n) average but O(n^2) worst case and needs the whole array in memory; heapq.nlargest(k, nums)[-1] also works.

questions.prompt: Which pair of structures gives O(1) get and O(1) put for an LRU cache with eviction?

options.text: A hash map from key to node, plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency.
options.why: Right: the map finds the node in O(1) and the doubly linked list unlinks and moves it to the front in O(1).

options.text: A hash map from key to node, plus a singly linked list ordered by recency.
options.why: Unlinking a node needs its predecessor, which a singly linked list can only find by walking, O(n).

options.text: A TreeMap keyed by last-access timestamp, plus a hash map from key to value.
options.why: Every access re-inserts into a balanced tree, O(log n), not O(1).

options.text: A min-heap keyed by last-access time, plus a hash map from key to value.
options.why: A heap cannot update the priority of an arbitrary entry in O(1); it costs O(log n) or worse.

questions.explanation: This is LeetCode 146. Dummy head and tail sentinels remove the null checks. Java's LinkedHashMap(cap, 0.75f, true) with removeEldestEntry, and Python's OrderedDict.move_to_end, give the same behaviour out of the box.

questions.prompt: Write a Python class LRUCache using collections.OrderedDict with __init__(capacity), get(key) returning -1 on a miss, and put(key, value) that evicts the least recently used key when over capacity.
questions.starter:
from collections import OrderedDict

class LRUCache:

checks.label: uses an OrderedDict
marks a key as most recently used on access
evicts the oldest entry
returns -1 on a miss

questions.explanation: Both get and put are O(1). Interviewers often follow up with 'now do it without OrderedDict': that is the hash map plus doubly linked list design, which these checks do not accept. A put on an existing key must also refresh its recency.

questions.prompt: A tree has edges 1-2, 1-3, 2-4, 2-5, 4-6 and 5-7. How many edges are on its longest path between any two nodes (the diameter)?
questions.explanation: The path 6-4-2-5-7 has 4 edges, as does 6-4-2-1-3. Compute it in one DFS: for each node, the best path through it is leftHeight + rightHeight; return 1 + max of the two to the parent. O(n) time, O(h) stack.
